headline_marked: [[Mahbubul Alam Hanif]] sentenced to death for 6 Kushtia murders
headline: Mahbubul Alam Hanif sentenced to death for 6 Kushtia murders
summary: Awami League Joint General Secretary Mahbubul Alam Hanif has been sentenced to death for his role in the killing of six people during the July Uprising in Kushtia. Three other party leaders received life sentences.
details: Awami League Joint General Secretary Mahbubul Alam Hanif has been sentenced to death for the killing of six people in Kushtia during the July Uprising. Three other party leaders, Kushtia district Awami League President Sadruddin Khan, district Awami League General Secretary Azgar Ali, and Kushtia city Awami League General Secretary Ataur Rahman Ata, were sentenced to jail until death.

The International Crimes Tribunal-2 pronounced the verdict, sentencing the four accused who are absconding. The tribunal also ordered the confiscation of half of the immovable property of all four convicted leaders, with proceeds to be distributed as compensation to victims.

The charges against Hanif and the other three leaders stemmed from their alleged endorsement of provocative statements and incitement of violence against protesters during July and August 2024. Hanif allegedly described protesters as Jamaat activists and criminals, encouraging lethal force against them.

The prosecution stated that Hanif's statements facilitated the use of lethal weapons, resulting in over 1,400 deaths and 25,000 injuries nationwide. Specifically in Kushtia on August 5, 2024, six protesters were shot dead and many others injured, with Hanif and the other leaders allegedly playing a role in these killings.

The tribunal framed three charges against the four leaders on November 2, 2025. The prosecution argued that acting on directives, the accused, with police support, ordered local leaders and activists to open fire on unarmed protesters in Kushtia city.

headline_marked: 47% of households [[borrow money to survive]] rising costs
headline: 47% of households borrow money to survive rising costs
summary: A BBS survey reveals a widening gap between average monthly income and expenditure, forcing many families to cut food and medical care.
details: A special survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) reveals that 47.42 per cent of households are borrowing money to meet rising living expenses.
The survey highlights a growing gap between income and spending. Average monthly household income is Tk 33,513, while average monthly expenditure has reached Tk 35,311.
Many families are forced to make difficult choices, such as reducing food purchases or delaying essential medical treatment to survive.
For low-income workers, the pressure is extreme. One city corporation cleaner in Dhaka reports skipping meals and eating leftovers to manage debt and rising utility costs.
The cost of LPG cylinders has surged, with prices rising from approximately Tk 1,550 to Tk 2,400, adding further strain on limited budgets.
Even middle-income households are struggling. Some report having to take new loans to repay existing ones as utility bills and service charges increase.
Families are now avoiding doctor visits and cutting out specific food items when prices spike to keep their monthly budgets manageable.
caption:
Nearly half of all Bangladeshi households are now borrowing money just to get by.

A special survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) reveals that 47.42 per cent of households are borrowing money to meet rising living expenses.

The survey highlights a growing gap between income and spending. Average monthly household income is Tk 33,513, while average monthly expenditure has reached Tk 35,311.

Many families are forced to make difficult choices, such as reducing food purchases or delaying essential medical treatment to survive.

For low-income workers, the pressure is extreme. One city corporation cleaner in Dhaka reports skipping meals and eating leftovers to manage debt and rising utility costs.

The cost of LPG cylinders has surged, with prices rising from approximately Tk 1,550 to Tk 2,400, adding further strain on limited budgets.

Even middle-income households are struggling. Some report having to take new loans to repay existing ones as utility bills and service charges increase.

Families are now avoiding doctor visits and cutting out specific food items when prices spike to keep their monthly budgets manageable.
